predictions.explanation:
The prediction was explicitly conditional: *if* Joe Biden were the 2024 Democratic nominee running against Donald Trump, then Biden would lose to Trump.

In reality, that condition never occurred:
- Joe Biden initially ran for re‑election and secured the primary delegates but **withdrew from the race on July 21, 2024**. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_elections?utm_source=openai))
- After Biden’s withdrawal, **Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee**, and she, not Biden, ran against Donald Trump in the November 5, 2024 election. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_elections?utm_source=openai))
- Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris, winning 312 electoral votes to 226 and a narrow popular‑vote plurality. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))

Because Biden was *not* the Democratic nominee facing Trump, the antecedent of the forecast (“Biden is the nominee vs. Trump in 2024”) was false. The actual world does not test the specific scenario the speaker predicted. While one could debate the counterfactual (what *would* have happened if Biden had stayed in and run), that outcome is unknowable from observed data.

Therefore, the prediction cannot be cleanly labeled as correct or incorrect based on real‑world results; it remains a statement about a hypothetical scenario that never materialized, so the appropriate resolution is **ambiguous**.

predictions.explanation:
Across the first two years after the November 2023 prediction, U.S. relations with **Iran**, **North Korea**, and **China (especially over Taiwan)** have not evolved in a clearly *more positive and stable* direction than the already‑pessimistic commentary at the time; in key cases they have instead moved toward the darker scenarios that many analysts warned about.

**1. Iran: from maximum pressure to open war and U.S. strikes**  
* In early 2025, Washington formally reinstated a “maximum pressure” sanctions campaign and explicitly threatened military action if nuclear talks failed, as Iran rapidly advanced enrichment toward weapons‑grade levels.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-set-reimpose-maximum-pressure-iran-official-says-2025-02-04/?utm_source=openai))  
* Negotiations in spring 2025 collapsed, and by June 2025 an **Iran–Israel war** broke out, featuring massive Iranian missile and drone strikes on Israel and Israeli attacks on Iranian territory.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2024_Iranian_strikes_on_Israel?utm_source=openai))  
* The U.S. directly entered the conflict with **Operation Midnight Hammer**, a large air and missile strike on three key Iranian nuclear facilities (Fordow, Natanz, Isfahan) — the first U.S. attacks on Iranian territory since the 1980s. Iran retaliated against a U.S. base in Qatar, and its cooperation with the IAEA deteriorated further.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_strikes_on_Iranian_nuclear_sites?utm_source=openai))  
* European officials and media had been warning in advance that a U.S. or Israeli strike on Iran’s nuclear program could make regional war “almost inevitable,” which is very close to what actually unfolded.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/iran-foreign-minister-attacking-our-nuclear-sites-would-be-one-biggest-mistakes-2025-01-31/?utm_source=openai))  

Taken together, U.S.–Iran relations have clearly **deteriorated into open armed confrontation**, not moved into a brighter, more stable future than gloomy analysts expected.

**2. North Korea: accelerating nuclear buildup, no diplomatic thaw**  
* Since 2023, North Korea has continued intensive missile testing, including new solid‑fuel intermediate‑range and intercontinental systems such as **Hwasong‑16B** (tested 2024 and 2025) and the new **Hwasong‑20** solid‑fuel ICBM revealed and paraded in 2025.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwasong-16B?utm_source=openai))  
* North Korea carried out record‑length ICBM tests in late 2024 designed to threaten the U.S. mainland, prompting strong condemnation from Washington, Tokyo, and Seoul and expanded U.S.–ROK–Japan military drills.([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/10/31/north-korea-launches-a-new-intercontinental-ballistic-missile-designed-to-threaten-us.html?utm_source=openai))  
* Pyongyang has explicitly rejected denuclearization talks, insisting the U.S. accept it as a permanent nuclear‑weapons state, and has denounced U.S.–South Korea–Japan security cooperation as hostile.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/north-korea-denounces-absurd-denuclearisation-pledge-by-us-allies-2025-02-18/?utm_source=openai))  

There has been **no meaningful improvement in political relations or stability** between Washington and Pyongyang; the trend is toward a more capable North Korean nuclear force and ongoing military confrontation, again matching or exceeding the negative expectations of many analysts.

**3. China and Taiwan: continued rivalry, higher military tension despite some tactical stabilizations**  
* Strategic assessments in 2024–25 consistently describe U.S.–China relations as **strained, competitive, and largely devoid of positive ambition**, with policymakers on both sides mainly focused on managing escalation risks rather than improving ties.([brookings.edu](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-does-national-confidence-inform-us-china-relations/?utm_source=openai))  
* Around Taiwan, PLA air and naval activities near the island and across its air defense zones have become more frequent and intense; Taiwan has condemned nearby live‑fire drills and incursions as major threats to regional peace.([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/e74bd7d6fc18ba8cf6780b4ca0831209?utm_source=openai))  
* In response, Taipei has announced a vast **$40 billion multi‑year defense buildup** explicitly aimed at countering China’s “intensifying” threats, while U.S. commanders and analysts continue to warn that China may be able to invade by around 2027.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/nov/26/taiwan-extra-40bn-defence-spending-china-threat?utm_source=openai))  
* Economically and technologically, the U.S. has tightened export controls and removed fast‑track status for chipmaking exports to Chinese fabs, while China has retaliated with restrictions on critical materials — deepening structural rivalry rather than easing it.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-revokes-tsmcs-fast-track-china-export-status-controls-tighten-2025-09-02/?utm_source=openai))  
* There *are* modest “technical” improvements — more direct flights, some resumed dialogues, and even announced plans for reciprocal Trump–Xi state visits — but these operate within a broader framework of ongoing strategic confrontation, not a clearly brighter overall relationship.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_route_authority_between_the_United_States_and_China?utm_source=openai))  

Meanwhile, prominent commentary during and after 2023 continued to warn that U.S.–China rivalry over Taiwan is one of the most likely triggers for World War III or a major great‑power war, underscoring how pessimistic the baseline discourse already was.([freenetafrica.com](https://freenetafrica.com/2025/09/30/global-flashpoints-the-imminent-threat-of-world-war-iii/?utm_source=openai))  Yet the actual trajectory since late 2023 has been **continued militarization and heightened perceived war risk**, not a clearly more stable or reassuring path than those warnings implied.

**Overall assessment**  
Because:

* U.S.–Iran relations have deteriorated into a hot regional war and direct U.S. strikes on Iranian territory;  
* U.S.–North Korea relations feature an expanded DPRK nuclear and missile arsenal, more tests, and an explicit rejection of denuclearization talks; and  
* U.S.–China relations remain structurally adversarial, with rising military tension over Taiwan and deepening techno‑economic conflict, only partly offset by limited tactical engagement;

…the evidence through November 30, 2025 indicates that these relationships have **not** evolved in a way that is *more positive and stable than widely anticipated by pessimistic commentators*. If anything, Iran and North Korea have moved squarely into the kind of severe‑deterioration scenarios those commentators feared, while China–U.S. ties remain tense and fragile. On the available record, that makes the prediction **wrong** rather than merely unproven or ambiguous at this point.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction is a broad *risk ranking* about what kinds of threats are “most likely” and “most threatening” to the United States in the “foreseeable future.” That kind of claim is inherently hard to falsify or verify, because:

1. **It’s about probability, not a concrete event.**  
   The statement compares *likelihood and severity* of categories of harm (cyber, information, biological vs. kinetic military attack). We don’t have an objective, agreed‑upon metric that tells us: “as of now, X category was definitively the most likely and threatening since November 2023.” Intelligence community threat assessments treat these as analytical judgments, not binary facts.

2. **Official U.S. assessments do emphasize cyber/information/biological as top threats, but without clean rankings vs. kinetic war.**  
   Recent unclassified U.S. intelligence and defense documents consistently describe cyber operations, disinformation, and potential pandemics/biothreats as *major* or even *top* national‑security threats, especially from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, and note how these can directly harm critical infrastructure, democratic processes, and public health. At the same time, they also stress the growing risk of great‑power military conflict and kinetic attacks (e.g., in the Indo‑Pacific or Europe) as existential or catastrophic risks. Because these reports do not give a definitive, numeric ranking that clearly puts cyber/social/biological *above* kinetic threats, they don’t let us decisively say the prediction is correct or incorrect.

3. **No decisive real‑world event has clearly disproved the claim.**  
   Since November 2023 there has been no large‑scale kinetic military attack on the U.S. homeland on the order of 9/11 or a major interstate war directly on U.S. territory. But the absence of such an attack does not prove that kinetic risks weren’t actually more likely or more threatening; it only shows they didn’t materialize in that time window. Likewise, while there have been ongoing cyber intrusions, ransomware incidents, influence operations, and persistent concern about future pandemics, we cannot cleanly measure that these were *objectively* more likely or more threatening than kinetic conflict in a way that settles the prediction.

4. **The time horizon (“foreseeable future”) is vague.**  
   “Foreseeable future” is not defined; it could reasonably extend well beyond late 2025. Without a clear time horizon, we cannot say “enough time has passed” to judge the prediction definitively.

Because the claim is (a) probabilistic, (b) comparative across very different threat domains, and (c) tied to an undefined time horizon, there is no rigorous, objective way at this point to say it has been clearly validated or falsified. Therefore, the fairest classification is **“ambiguous”** rather than right, wrong, or merely “too early.”
predictions.grok_explanation: No direct foreign kinetic military attacks on the US homeland occurred between Nov 2023 and Dec 2025, per searches on kinetic attacks (results focused on US strikes abroad, e.g., on drug boats or Somalia). In contrast, significant cyber harms materialized: Chinese hackers breached US gov/infra (CSIS Significant Cyber Incidents, Jul 2025); massive breaches like Microsoft Exchange affecting 30k businesses (UpGuard); ransomware dominant (SentinelOne). Information warfare peaked during 2024 election with Russian/Chinese/Iranian disinformation (Brookings, NPR, DOJ disruptions). Biological threats loomed in assessments (DNI ATA 2025, DHS HTA 2025) but no major incidents. Threat reports (DNI, DIA 2025) prioritize cyber/influence/bio over kinetic risks to US, aligning with the prediction.

predictions.explanation:
As of 30 November 2025, China is experiencing a serious and ongoing property- and debt-driven downturn—Evergrande’s collapse and court‑ordered liquidation, the distress of major developers like Country Garden, falling home prices, and a shrinking real‑estate share of GDP all point to a substantial bubble that has been deflating over several years. 【0search14】【0news15】

However, this has **not yet produced a discrete financial crisis that is clearly larger in scale and severity than the 2008 U.S./global financial crisis**:

- China’s overall GDP has continued to grow at around 5% in 2023–2024, and the IMF still projects positive, if slowing, growth rather than a deep recession. 【1search1】
- By contrast, the 2008 crisis led to a 4.3% peak‑to‑trough contraction in U.S. real GDP and a doubling of unemployment to about 10%, with massive wealth losses and a sharp global recession. 【1search2】【1search19】

So the *specific* claim that China will have a bubble burst that **“will make [the 2008 crisis] look like a gumball”** has **not come true yet**, but the prediction is also **not definitively falsified**, because the speaker did not specify a time horizon and China’s structural property and local‑government‑debt problems are still unfolding. 【1search1】

Given that a clearly worse‑than‑2008 crash has not occurred, but may still occur in the future and no explicit deadline was attached to the prediction, the fairest classification as of late 2025 is **“inconclusive (too early to tell).”**
predictions.grok_explanation: China has faced an ongoing real estate slump since 2021 (e.g., Evergrande default), with property prices falling (fastest pace in 11 months in Sep 2025 per Reuters), new home sales down ~24% YoY in Jul 2025, and fixed-asset investment shrinking 1.7% in first 10 months of 2025 (Bloomberg). Stock markets saw sharp drops (worst single-day since 2008 in Apr 2025, worst week in years in 2024 per Guardian/CNN). However, no major economic/financial bubble bursting larger than 2008 has occurred: GDP grew ~5% in 2024 and ~4.8% in 2025 Q3 (Trading Economics, IMF, National Bureau of Statistics); unemployment stable ~5% (Statista, Macrotrends); no systemic bank failures or global contagion like 2008 (US GDP contracted -2.5%, unemployment 10%). Instead, slowdown/deflation risks akin to Japan (Bruegel, CSIS: 'stumbles but unlikely to fall'). Sources: IMF F&D, CSIS Sep 2025, Trading Economics GDP/unemployment, Reuters property data.

predictions.explanation:
Available evidence since November 2023 shows that U.S. land borders remain heavily used by foreign nationals from adversarial or high‑risk countries and that senior officials explicitly describe this as a vulnerability that *could* be exploited by adversaries—but public sources do **not** clearly document state‑directed infiltration campaigns that would definitively confirm the prediction.

**What has clearly happened:**
- The U.S. Border Patrol chief has called the southern border a *“national security threat,”* emphasizing more than a million annual apprehensions and about 140,000 “known got‑aways” in just a few months, and saying that unknown actors are *“exploiting a vulnerability that’s on our border right now.”* ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jason-owens-border-patrol-southern-border-national-security-threat/?utm_source=openai))
- Congressional and committee reports show a sharp rise in encounters with people on the terrorist watchlist at U.S. borders during FY 2022–2024 (hundreds versus low double digits in earlier years), highlighting concern that individuals tied to terrorist networks are using these routes. ([dailysignal.com](https://www.dailysignal.com/2024/08/06/99-illegal-aliens-on-terrorist-watchlist-released-into-us-report-finds/?utm_source=openai))
- Reporting has revealed specific cases, such as an Afghan national on the U.S. terrorist watchlist who crossed the southern border, was apprehended and released into the interior, and later re‑arrested—illustrating that at least some suspected extremists have entered via porous border processes. ([hstoday.us](https://www.hstoday.us/subject-matter-areas/border-security/man-on-terror-watchlist-was-released-by-border-patrol/?utm_source=openai))
- At the same time, congressional hearings and media coverage have focused on a historic surge in Chinese nationals crossing illegally between ports of entry, with lawmakers and security officials explicitly warning that the People’s Republic of China—described as a top U.S. adversary—could use these flows to embed intelligence operatives or other hostile actors. ([homeland.house.gov](https://homeland.house.gov/2024/05/16/a-serious-national-security-concern-subcommittee-chairman-bishop-opens-hearing-on-surge-of-chinese-nationals-illegally-crossing-the-border/?utm_source=openai))
- Separate incidents, such as Chinese nationals attempting to enter Guam illegally near a U.S. missile test site, have raised concrete espionage concerns tied to border or perimeter breaches, reinforcing that foreign intelligence services test and probe U.S. access controls. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/seven-chinese-nationals-tried-illegally-enter-guam-us-tested-missile-authorities-2024-12-21/?utm_source=openai))

**Why this does not cleanly settle the prediction:**
- Publicly available information typically stops at **suspicion** or **risk assessment**: officials and analysts warn that terrorists or hostile states *may* be exploiting border weaknesses, and they highlight watchlist encounters and suspicious incidents, but they rarely disclose definitive proof that specific illegal entrants were directed by foreign governments or organizations as part of an organized infiltration strategy.
- Many crossings from adversarial countries appear driven by economic or personal motives, and the government has not (in public) tied the post‑2023 surge to a coordinated foreign campaign that exploits U.S. political dysfunction per se.

Because we can clearly see that the borders are heavily stressed and treated as a national‑security vulnerability, and that some individuals of security concern have entered this way, the prediction is **plausible** and partially aligned with observable trends. However, given the lack of unambiguous, declassified proof that foreign adversaries have systematically used the porous borders for directed infiltration in the way implied, the outcome cannot be firmly labeled as either fully ‘right’ or ‘wrong’. It remains **ambiguous** based on open sources.

As of November 30, 2025, Benjamin Netanyahu is still the Prime Minister of Israel, and no new Knesset election has yet taken place that removed him from office.

Key points:

- Netanyahu returned to office as Prime Minister on December 29, 2022, heading Israel’s 37th government.
- After the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, there were extensive protests and calls for his resignation, but his government remained in power.
- The next regular Knesset election is not scheduled until late 2026, and as of late 2025 no early election has been held and no successor has replaced Netanyahu as Prime Minister.

Because the prediction stated that *in the near term after October 7, 2023* Israel would hold new elections in which Netanyahu would be replaced as Prime Minister, and this has not occurred by November 30, 2025, the prediction is **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction is conditional and counterfactual: B is asserting that **if** the U.S. *were to adopt* a reciprocity-based and uniform regulatory standard for social media and digital platforms, then some major platforms that fail to meet those standards would be banned from operating in the U.S.

To evaluate this, we would need both:

1. The U.S. to have actually adopted something that clearly qualifies as a **reciprocity-based and uniform regulatory standard** for all social/digital platforms, and
2. As a result of that standard, some **major platforms** to have been **banned from operating in the U.S.**

As of November 30, 2025, the U.S. has not enacted a comprehensive, EU-style, uniform, reciprocity-driven platform regime of the sort described (there is a patchwork of laws and proposals like Section 230 reforms, state privacy laws, kids’ online safety bills, and various content-moderation debates, but not a single reciprocity standard that applies identically to all platforms). There have also not been outright nationwide bans of multiple major platforms under such a regime. TikTok has faced high-profile federal and state-level restrictions and attempted bans, typically grounded in national security and data concerns, not in a **reciprocity-based uniform standard** across *all* platforms.

Because the **trigger condition** of the prediction (the U.S. adopting the specific kind of regulatory framework B is imagining) has not occurred, we cannot observe whether B’s claimed consequence (major non‑compliant platforms being banned) would actually follow. That makes the truth of the underlying causal claim impossible to verify empirically.

So, the prediction cannot be classified as right or wrong based on real‑world outcomes; it remains a hypothetical about a scenario that never materialized, which makes it **ambiguous** rather than simply premature or falsified.
predictions.grok_explanation: The U.S. has not adopted a reciprocity-based and uniform regulatory standard for social media and digital platforms that would ban non-compliant major platforms. No major platforms (e.g., Facebook, X/Twitter, Instagram) have been banned nationwide. The 'China Social Media Reciprocity Act' (H.R.8041, 117th Congress) was introduced in 2022 but not passed ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/8041)). TikTok faced a 2024 divestiture law (PAFACA), upheld by SCOTUS Jan 2025, but enforcement delayed multiple times by Trump executive orders to Dec 16, 2025, with a deal framework for U.S. operations; it remains operational ([White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/09/further-extending-the-tiktok-enforcement-delay-9dde/), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/tiktok-lives-us-china-deal-app-keep-operating-us-2025-09-16/), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restrictions_on_TikTok_in_the_United_States)). TikTok action is national security-specific, not uniform/reciprocity-based across all platforms. State laws target minors' access or devices, not bans ([Exploding Topics](https://explodingtopics.com/blog/banned-social-media-apps)). Over 2 years post-podcast (Nov 2023), scenario unrealized.

predictions.explanation:
As of 30 November 2025, Vladimir Putin is still the president of Russia, and there has been no clearly defined "post-Putin era" to evaluate. Current news and reference sources continue to describe him as Russia’s president and de facto leader.

Because the prediction is explicitly about *"a post-putin Russia"* becoming a failed nation with severe brain drain, it concerns conditions **after** Putin has left power. Since that transition has not occurred yet, there is no way to judge whether Russia *will* be a failed state in that future scenario.

Even though Russia has experienced substantial emigration of educated and skilled workers since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 (often described as a major brain drain in media and analyses), that is not sufficient to assess a forecast specifically tied to the *post-Putin* period. The relevant time frame simply hasn’t happened yet.

Therefore the correct status for this prediction is: it’s **too early to tell**.

No evidence of him leaving power. Thus, too early to assess if post-Putin Russia becomes a failed state. Current brain drain exists due to Ukraine war (~650k outflow, [Carnegie](https://carnegieendowment.org/russia-eurasia/politika/2025/09/russia-new-demographic-crisis?lang=en)), but Russia persists as a functional wartime state ([CSIS](https://www.csis.org/analysis/russias-war-ukraine-next-chapter), [WaPo](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2025/11/25/russia-ukraine-war-offensive-2025/)).

predictions.explanation: At the time of the podcast (November 17, 2023), a CNN/UNH poll of likely New Hampshire Democratic primary voters had Joe Biden at about 65% and Dean Phillips at 10%, and reported that 41% had not heard he was running and roughly three-quarters did not know enough about him to hold an opinion, indicating low initial support and visibility. ([keyt.com](https://keyt.com/politics/cnn-us-politics/2023/11/17/cnn-poll-new-hampshire-democrats-see-biden-as-partys-best-shot-to-hold-white-house/)) Over the following month, American Research Group’s tracking of likely New Hampshire Democratic primary voters showed Phillips rising from 17% on December 20 to 21%, 26%, 28%, and then 32% by January 20, while Biden remained in the mid‑50s, a clear upward trend. ([americanresearchgroup.com](https://americanresearchgroup.com/pres2024/dem/nhdem.html?utm_source=openai)) Other pollsters in January also found him in the mid‑single to mid‑teens (for example, 7–10% in CNN/UNH, 16% in Emerson), confirming that his support was meaningfully higher than at launch even if estimates differed. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Hampshire_Democratic_presidential_primary?utm_source=openai)) Reporting just before the primary noted that some surveys had Phillips around 28% to Biden’s 58% and described him as having found “some momentum” in the state. ([startribune.com](https://www.startribune.com/dean-phillips-seeks-upset-win-against-biden-in-new-hampshire-primary/600337534?utm_source=openai)) In the January 23, 2024 New Hampshire Democratic primary itself, Phillips ultimately received about 19–20% of the vote, a distant second to Biden’s write‑in total of about 64% but roughly double his mid‑November polling and far above his initial, near‑unknown status. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Hampshire_Democratic_presidential_primary?utm_source=openai)) Nationally, he never rose beyond low single digits and soon ended his campaign after weak results elsewhere, so he did not broadly transform the race. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Phillips_2024_presidential_campaign?utm_source=openai)) However, Chamath’s specific claim was that Phillips’ numbers, particularly in New Hampshire, would improve significantly as more voters saw him. Given the substantial polling gains there and a final vote share around 20% from a very low starting point, that prediction about his New Hampshire polling trajectory is supported by the outcomes.

predictions.grok_explanation: Chamath predicted Dean Phillips' polling in New Hampshire would improve significantly with increased visibility and grassroots efforts during the 2024 Democratic primary cycle. Around the podcast date (Nov 17, 2023), a UNH/CNN poll (Nov 10-14) showed Phillips at 10% vs. Biden's 65%. Subsequent polls were volatile but showed gains in several: e.g., ARG (Dec 14-20) 17%, ARG (Dec 27-Jan 4) 21%, ARG (Jan 12-15) 28%, ARG (Jan 18-20) 32%. In the Jan 23, 2024, primary, Phillips received 19.7% (24,377 votes) vs. Biden's write-in 63.8% (79,100 votes), a strong second-place finish for a late entrant, doubling his mid-November polling and validating the prediction of pulling well in NH grassroots context. Phillips viewed 20% as success ([KARE11](https://www.kare11.com/article/news/politics/phillips-bets-it-all-on-new-hampshire-primary/89-21553088-2eeb-4497-93f4-48d359eebe03)). Sources: [Wikipedia polling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Hampshire_Democratic_presidential_primary), [NYT results](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/01/23/us/elections/results-new-hampshire-democratic-primary.html), UNH poll Nov 2023.

predictions.explanation:
* Joe Biden formally announced he would seek reelection in 2024 and proceeded to run in the Democratic primaries, where he **won an overwhelming majority of delegates and became the presumptive Democratic nominee**, easily defeating challengers including Rep. Dean Phillips. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))
* Dean Phillips mounted a long-shot primary challenge focused largely on Biden’s age, but he performed poorly (e.g., about 20% in New Hampshire while Biden won via write‑in) and failed to gain traction in subsequent contests like South Carolina. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/a899f4ee06b06406c93c3896362aaf05?utm_source=openai))
* On March 6, 2024, Phillips **ended his campaign and endorsed Biden**, explicitly acknowledging that he was not the alternative Democratic voters wanted. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/dean-phillips-ends-2024-challenge-biden-with-endorsement-2024-03-06/?utm_source=openai))
* Only after Biden had already secured effective control of the delegate race and become the presumptive nominee did he later withdraw from the 2024 general election on July 21, 2024; Vice President Kamala Harris was then made the Democratic nominee. This later withdrawal does not change the fact that Phillips never defeated Biden for the Democratic nomination and, in practice, never came close to doing so. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))

Because Biden did run in the 2024 Democratic primaries and Phillips was unable to seriously challenge, let alone defeat, him for the nomination, Friedberg’s prediction that Phillips “doesn’t stand a chance” against Biden under those structural conditions was borne out by events.

Dean Phillips suspended his campaign on March 6, 2024, after failing to win any primaries (e.g., AP News: 'ended his long-shot 2024 Democratic presidential bid... after failing to win a primary contest'; PBS, CBS News, NBC News, Politico). predictions.explanation:
Joe Biden ultimately **did not remain in the 2024 presidential race**: he ended his reelection campaign in July 2024 and withdrew from the race, with major outlets reporting his decision not to seek reelection and to step aside as the Democratic nominee. 

Since Sacks’s prediction was effectively that *Biden would run and not drop out before the general election* with a probability of about 70% (i.e., the more-likely outcome in his view), and the opposite outcome occurred (Biden did drop out before the general election), this specific prediction is counted as **wrong** in outcome terms.
predictions.grok_explanation: Joe Biden announced his withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race on July 21, 2024, well before the general election on November 5, 2024, and endorsed Kamala Harris as the Democratic nominee. This directly contradicts the prediction that there was a 70% chance he would remain in the race and not drop out before the general election. Sources: [Wikipedia: Withdrawal of Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election), [AP News](https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2024/biden-drops-out-of-2024-race-after-disastrous-debate-inflamed-age-concerns-vp-harris-gets-his-nod/), [CNN: 2024 Presidential Candidates](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2024/politics/presidential-candidates-dg/).

predictions.explanation: Chamath predicted that by February or March 2024, the year-over-year U.S. CPI inflation rate would be in the low‑2% range, around 2.2%. In reality, official Bureau of Labor Statistics data show headline CPI was **3.2%** year-over-year in February 2024 and **3.5%** in March 2024—about a full percentage point above his forecast and still well above the Fed’s 2% target. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2024/consumer-prices-up-3-2-percent-from-february-2023-to-february-2024.htm?utm_source=openai)) Therefore, the prediction was wrong.

predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction was for U.S. CPI YoY inflation to be in the low-2% range (~2.2%) by Feb or Mar 2024. Actual figures: **Feb 2024: 3.2%**, **Mar 2024: 3.5%** (both CPI-U all items, not seasonally adjusted, standard headline YoY). These are in the mid-3% range, not low-2%.
